records.abstract: Stomach contents of 112 bycaught harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) collected between 1989 and 1996 in the Kattegat and Skagerrak seas were analyzed to describe diet composition and estimate prey size, to examine sample size requirements, and to compare juvenile and adult diets. Although porpoises preyed on a variety of species, only a few contributed substantially to the diet. Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) was the dominating prey species for both juveniles and adults. Our results, in combination with those from previous studies, suggest that where herring is a dominant food source, porpoises prey primarily on size classes containing mature or maturing individuals. Further, we also show that Atlantic hagfish (Myxine glutinosa) may be an important food resource, at least for adult porpoises. Examination of sample size requirement showed that, depending on the taxonomic level used to describe the diet, a minimum of 35–71 stomachs are needed to be confident that all common prey species will be found.
records.title: Diet of harbour porpoises in the Kattegat and Skagerrak Seas: Accounting for individual variation and sample size.

records.abstract: The diving behaviour of seven free-ranging harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) was examined using time–depth recorders. In total, 8167 individual dives were recorded over 254 h. The longest period of data collection from an individual was 106.1 h. Mean dive depths and durations ranged from 14 ± 16 to 41 ± 32 m, and from 44 ± 37 to 103 ± 67 s, respectively. The maximum recorded dive depth and duration was 226 m and 321 s. This performance may not represent the maximum capacity of harbour porpoises but rather the maximum depth of the study area. Individual dives had similar rates of descent and ascent, which ranged from 1.1 ± 0.6 to 2.3 ± 1.4 m/s, and from 0.9 ± 0.6 to 2.1 ± 1.4 m/s, respectively. Two porpoises with monitoring periods >2 days demonstrated a diel pattern in their diving, making fewer, but deeper dives at night. Comparison of the diving behaviour of harbour porpoises with data on the depth of 140 porpoises entanglements in groundfish gill nets in the Bay of Fundy showed these seven porpoises made between 22 and 70% of dives to depths (range 20–130 m) where the majority of entanglements were reported.
records.title: Diving behaviour of harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) in the Bay of Fundy

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Pinnipeds have been blamed for the lack of recovery of fishes of human importance. Removing artificial haul‐out sites has been proposed to reduce pinniped presence and presumably predation. However, the effectiveness of this nonlethal management method has not been examined. We analyzed harbor seal ( Phoca vitulina ) numbers at two sites in Bellingham, WA, USA, where seals haul out on floating haul‐out structures adjacent to Whatcom Creek, used by Pacific salmon ( Oncorhynchus spp.). We used Generalized Additive Mixed Models ( GAMMs ) with a continuous‐time AR(1) correlation structure to predict seasonal and interannual trends in seal counts at the haul‐out sites and Whatcom Creek before (pre‐2015), during (2015–2022), and after (post‐2022) floating haul‐out removal. Model‐predicted haul‐outs at Log Pond peaked at 33.3 seals in 2013 (95% CI: 26.9–41.1), declined by 90% to 3.4 seals in 2017 (95% CI: 2.4–4.8), rose by 101% to 6.8 seals in 2019 (95% CI: 5.1–9.1), and declined to near zero seals in 2023 (95% CI: 0.0–0.0). At Creek, model‐predicted seal counts increased by 135% from 2.4 seals in 2011 (95% CI: 1.9–3.2) to 5.8 seals in 2021 (95% CI: 5.1–6.4). The 2011–2021 increase in model‐predicted seals at Whatcom Creek was followed by a 6% decrease to 5.4 seals in 2023 (95% CI: 4.6–6.4). These predominantly divergent trends between hauled‐out seals and seals swimming in Whatcom Creek suggest that removing artificial haul‐out structures may reduce the number of hauled‐out seals at targeted sites without necessarily reducing seal counts in adjacent foraging habitat.
records.title: Temporal Trends in Harbor Seal ( Phoca vitulina ) Counts Throughout Removal of Artificial Haul‐Out Sites Adjacent to Critical Salmon Habitat

records.abstract: Summary1The status of small cetaceans in the North Sea and adjacent waters has been of concern for many years. Shipboard and aerial line transect surveys were conducted to provide accurate and precise estimates of abundance as a basis for conservation strategy in European waters.2The survey, known as SCANS (Small Cetacean Abundance in the North Sea), was conducted in summer 1994 and designed to generate precise and unbiased abundance estimates. Thus the intensity of survey was high, and data collection and analysis methods allowed for the probability of detection of animals on the transect line being less than unity and, for shipboard surveys, also allowed for animal movement in response to the survey platform.3Shipboard transects covered 20 000 km in an area of 890 000 km2. Aerial transects covered 7000 km in an area of 150 000 km2.4Three species dominated the data. Harbour porpoise Phocoena phocoena were encountered throughout the survey area except in the Channel and the southern North Sea. Whitebeaked dolphin Lagenorhynchus albirostris and minke whale Balaenoptera acutorostrata were found mainly in the north-western North Sea.5Phocoena phocoena abundance for the entire survey area was estimated as 341 366 [coefficient of variation (CV) = 0·14; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 260 000–449 000]. The estimated number of B. acutorostrata was 8445 (CV = 0·24; 95% CI 5000–13 500). The estimate for L. albirostris based on confirmed sightings of this species was 7856 (CV = 0·30; 95% CI = 4000–13 000). When Atlantic whitesided dolphin Lagenorhynchusacutus and Lagenorhynchus spp. sightings were included, this estimate increased to 11 760 (CV = 0·26; 95% CI 5900–18 500).6Shortbeaked common dolphin Delphinus delphis were found almost exclusively in the Celtic Sea. Abundance was estimated as 75 450 (CV = 0·67; 95% CI = 23 000–149 000).7Current assessments and recommendations by international fora concerning the impact on P. phocoena of bycatch in gillnet fisheries in the North Sea and adjacent waters are based on these estimates.
records.title: Abundance of harbour porpoise and other cetaceans in the North Sea and adjacent waters

records.abstract: This study examined pituitary sensitivity to exogenous gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in relation to time of year and changes in plasma progesterone, testosterone, luteinising hormone (LH), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentrations during the annual cycle of adult and juvenile harbour seals (Phoca vitulina vitulina). There was no significant difference in seasonal changes in reproductive hormone levels between six captive individuals and seals caught from the wild (n = 80). Based on results from both the captive and the wild individuals, the plasma progesterone concentration was elevated in late gestation, whereas it declined at the equivalent time in nonpregnant females. The progesterone concentration was also elevated during the phase of delayed implantation, but there was no difference between pregnant and nonpregnant seals. In captive seals given exogenous GnRH, the LH concentration peaked 10-20 min after injection of GnRH, and the magnitude of the LH response depended upon the dose up to similar to 120 ng.kg(-1). FSH did not respond to GnRH in the time course of the experiment. Pituitary sensitivity to GnRH was greatest in the summer and autumn and lowest in the winter and spring. Seasonal changes in pituitary sensitivity were apparent in both adults and juveniles. There was evidence that three of the four juvenile seals attained puberty during the study. We conclude that the seasonal patterns of pituitary sensitivity and plasma hormone concentration in harbour seals are consistent with a reproductive cycle under photoperiodic control and with the general mechanisms underlying photoperiodic control of seasonal reproduction in higher vertebrates.
records.title: Changes in pituitary, ovarian, and testicular activity in harbour seals (Phoca vitulina) in relation to season and sexual maturity

records.abstract: Incidental mortality of harbour porpoises, Phocoena phocoena, from captures in ®shing gear has been documented consistently as severe in some European waters. Since fishing effort varies greatly among regions, management units must be designed for more effective conservation of this species. In this study, analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) restriction fragments was performed to investigate the population structure of harbour porpoises in the Baltic Sea, the joint Kattegat±Skagerrak Seas and off the west coast of Norway. Mitochondrial DNA of 65 harbour porpoises collected from three regions was analysed with nine restriction enzymes. Analysis of the heterogeneity in the frequency distribution of haplotypes among provisional subpopulations revealed signi®cant differences, which supports the recognition of three different subpopulations and thus three separate management units. Furthermore, indices of haplotypic diversity (range: 0.211 to 0.628) and nucleotide diversity (range: 0.070 to 0.168) of these provisional subpopulations were much lower than for western North Atlantic subpopulations, which is consistent with the view that harbour porpoises in European waters, particularly in the Baltic Sea, are depleted.
records.title: Mitochondrial DNA analysis of harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) to identify populations in the Baltic Sea, the Kattegatt-Skagerrak Seas and the North Sea

records.abstract: Abstract Animals are often trapped to learn more about a species’ behavioural ecology, either invasively with live traps or non-invasively with hair- or camera traps. The use of scent lures or baits can help to attract animals to the trap site. The aim of this study was to identify the best and most efficient trapping techniques and scent lure or bait for research on Eurasian otters ( Lutra lutra ). The systematic literature review, in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, was designed to include results for all otter species. It recovered 16 papers, most published between 2011 and 2020 covering six otter species. This review identified six different main trapping methods (net traps, leghold traps, cage traps as live- or hair traps, suitcase traps, hair traps using sticks, and camera traps). Scent lures were only utilized in the hair- and camera trapping studies. Due to the limited comparability of the studies, the most effective trapping or scent lure/bait method could not be concluded. The review therefore provides the pros and cons of these various capture techniques for otter research. This study highlights the need for more research on otter trapping focused on the use of scent lures or baits, trap placement, amounts of bycatch, and animal welfare to trap otters in the most effective and least harmful way.
records.title: Invasive or non-invasive trapping of otters and the use of scent lures and baits: a review

records.abstract: Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a pleiotropic cytokine that acts primarily on immune cells to regulate inflammatory, innate, and adaptive immune responses to maintain tissue homeostasis. Viruses have evolved mechanisms to manipulate immunosurveillance by their hosts. A common strategy is the genetic acquisition and production of host proteins such as IL-10. Many viruses have been reported to encode IL-10, including members of the Herpesviridae and Poxviridae. The viral IL-10 proteins have diversified in sequence and function relative to those of their host species, but generally inhibit immune function and promote infection. A prime example is the IL-10 protein produced by Orf virus (ORFV) from the Parapoxvirus (PPV) genus of Poxviridae, which shares the immune suppressive and immune stimulatory properties of hIL-10. Four additional PPV members, namely Pseudocowpox virus (PCPV), Bovine papular stomatitis virus (BPSV), Red deer parapoxvirus (RDPV) and Grey seal parapoxvirus (GSPV), have been reported to encode variants of IL-10. As prior studies of viral IL-10 proteins provided great insight into this family of proteins, it was hypothesised that investigations into the evolution, structure, and function of these natural IL-10 variants would increase understanding of viral IL-10s as virulence factors, host IL-10s as master regulators of immune function, and recombinant IL-10 proteins as therapeutics for immune-mediated diseases. To investigate the evolution of the viral IL-10 family, an updated list of viral and host IL-10s was compiled and phylogenetic analysis was performed. The 36 viral IL-10 proteins formed seven distinct clades, with varying evolutionary distances to the IL-10 proteins from their respective hosts. The PPV IL-10s formed one clade in the phylogenetic tree, clustering near each other and the IL-10s from humans and their mammalian hosts. To predict the structure of the PPV IL-10s, their amino acid sequences were aligned, revealing moderate levels of amino acid identity and similarity with human IL-10. Furthermore, structural models indicated the PPV IL-10s would adopt an overall tertiary structure analogous to hIL-10. This structural homology, in turn, suggested they would engage the IL-10 receptor complex in a similar manner to hIL-10. However, some variations in structure, glycosylation and receptor interactions were predicted between the PPV IL-10s and that of hIL-10, implying there could be differences in their downstream signalling and immunoregulatory effects. To facilitate functional analyses of the PPV IL-10s, recombinant proteins were expressed in a mammalian cell line and then purified using affinity chromatography. Purification of GSPV IL-10 proved particularly challenging, requiring method optimisation. Biochemical analysis of the purified PPV IL-10s revealed some interesting findings. The molecular weights for the ORFV, PCPV, and human IL-10s were higher than predicted and consistent with dimer formation. The RDPV and GSPV IL-10s also exhibited higher molecular weights than predicted, with N-glycosidase digestion confirming the presence of N-linked glycans. These biochemical differences between the human and PPV IL-10s could also influence their molecular interactions and biological effects. To investigate the immune suppressive and immune stimulatory functions of the PPV IL-10s, the recombinant proteins were applied to human monocytic and murine mast cells, stimulated with lipoteichoic acid (LTA) or IL-3 and IL-4, respectively. All PPV IL-10s retained some degree of immune-suppressive and immune-stimulatory activities analogous to hIL-10, however, the levels of these activities varied. The ORFV and BPSV IL-10s were the most potent and effective agonists of LTA-induced cytokine production by monocytes, and ORFV and RDPV IL-10s were the most potent and effective agonists of IL-3 and IL-4-stimulated mast cell proliferation. By contrast, the PCPV and GSPV IL-10s were partial agonists with reduced potency and efficacy in these cellular assays. These quantitative differences indicate that while the PPV IL-10s interact with the IL-10 receptor complex, they may vary in their molecular interactions and induction of signalling pathways. To investigate receptor binding by the PPV IL-10s, various methods were trialled with varying success. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer assays utilising a human cell line expressing various combinations of IL-10 receptor (IL-10R) detected IL-10R1-IL-10R1 homodimerisation in response to excessive amounts of hIL-10 but failed to detect IL-10R2-IL-10R2 homodimerisation, or IL-10R1-IL-10R2 heterodimerisation. Competitive binding assays utilising recombinant IL-10R-1 proteins detected concentration-dependent binding by human, ORFV, BPSV, PCPV and RDPV IL-10s, but not GSPV IL-10. Detection of IL-10R2 binding by hIL-10 required excessive receptor amounts. Co-immunoprecipitation of the human and PPV IL-10s with the recombinant receptors, followed by Western blot detection of each binding partner, supported the findings from the competitive IL-10R1 binding assay. It also revealed variable binding by the human and PPV IL-10s to IL-10R2, the greatest extent by BPSV IL-10, and the least by GSPV IL-10. However, when both IL-10Rs were included, competition was observed, with the level of each receptor interaction decreasing. Finally, the signalling pathways induced by the PPV IL-10s were examined in LTA-stimulated monocytes. Phosphorylation of STAT3 at tyrosine 705, for the most part, aligned with the receptor binding profiles of the human and PPV IL-10 in Western blot and AlphaLISA analyses, with the PCPV, BPSV and RDPV IL-10s showing the greatest potency, and the GSPV IL-10 being the least potent. Overall, the combined analyses revealed that the PPV IL-10 proteins share a common origin and structure, but have important differences in their biochemical properties, immunomodulatory functions, receptor interactions, and signalling responses. Taken together, these findings provide crucial insights into the structure-function relationship in the IL-10 family. This knowledge has implications for how viral IL-10s modulate host immunity to enable virus persistence and how host IL-10s control immune homeostasis. This study may lead to the development of the PPV IL-10s, or other modified IL-10s, as new, improved anti-inflammatory therapeutic agents.

records.abstract: Abstract Understanding small‐odontocete behaviour near static nets is central to reducing bycatch, the main source of anthropogenic mortality. The causes of bycatch however remain unknown due to a lack of direct observations of net–animal interactions. We conducted the first in situ drone‐ and acoustic‐based experiment examining harbour porpoise behaviour around a dummy bottom set net, deployed alone and in combination with an acoustic alerting device, describing movement patterns, quantifying swimming speeds and respiration rates, and echolocation responses. Porpoises frequently crossed the net swimming over the float‐line. The net and the alert device did not elicit strong changes in swimming speeds, respiration rates, or acoustic behaviour. Porpoises consistently avoided direct contact with the net at short observed reaction distances (0.8–16.4 m). Policy implications . Our findings suggest that bycatch is not simply due to a failure to detect nets but rather occurs when avoidance fails, highlighting the need for mitigation strategies that enhance detectability and support avoidance behaviour to overcome the global gillnet bycatch issue. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the journal's blog .
records.title: Avoidance failure, not detection failure drives gillnet bycatch in a small toothed whale: The harbour porpoise

records.abstract: Metabarcoding provides a powerful tool for investigating biodiversity and trophic interactions, but the high sensitivity of this methodology makes it vulnerable to errors, resulting in artefacts in the final data. Metabarcoding studies thus often utilise minimum sequence copy thresholds (MSCTs) to remove artefacts that remain in datasets; however, there is no consensus on best practice for the use of MSCTs. To mitigate erroneous reporting of results and inconsistencies, this study discusses and provides guidance for best-practice filtering of metabarcoding data for the ascertainment of conservative and accurate data. The most common MSCTs identified in the literature were applied to example datasets of Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) and cereal crop spider (Araneae: Linyphiidae and Lycosidae) diets. Changes in both the method and threshold value considerably affected the resultant data. Of the MSCTs tested, it was concluded that the optimal method for the examples given combined a sample-based threshold with removal of maximum taxon contamination, providing stringent filtering of artefacts whilst retaining target data. Choice of threshold value differed between datasets due to variation in artefact abundance and sequencing depth, thus studies should employ controls (mock communities, negative controls with no DNA and unused MID-tag combinations) to select threshold values appropriate for each individual study.
records.title: Post-bioinformatic methods to identify and reduce the prevalence of artefacts in metabarcoding data

records.abstract: San Francisco Bay Area Network Inventory and Monitoring Network Pinniped Monitoring Data Summary Data Package. The summary data package was derived from the Native Survey Scale Pinnipeds Data Package datasets that have been summarized via R script, see xml metadata for further details. Pinniped Monitoring background: Within the order Carnivora, the Pinnipedia sub-order is a group of marine mammals that includes sea lions, fur seals, true seals, and walruses. Pinnipeds are keystone species who serve as excellent indicators of marine ecosystem health because they respond quickly to changing oceanic conditions. Conservation concerns include effects of climate change, human disturbance, oil spills, fishing activities (operational and biological), natural and anthropogenically enhanced toxic algal blooms, preservation of haul out habitats, biomagnified contaminants, and disease. Monitoring focuses on the two numerically dominant pinniped species that breed, haul out, and molt in San Francisco Bay Area Network (SFAN) parks: the Pacific Harbor Seal (Phoca vitulina richardii) and Northern Elephant Seal (Mirounga angustirostris). This information contributes significantly to the regional and stock-wide understanding of these species required under the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972. Ancillary data on other pinniped species are collected concurrently, but are not the primary targets of this monitoring protocol. Monitoring is performed annually at two SFAN parks: Point Reyes National Seashore (PORE) and Golden Gate National Recreation Area (GOGA). Objectives are to 1) determine the long-term trends in population size and seasonal distribution of seal populations at primary sites in the SFAN parks during the breeding and molt seasons, 2) determine long-term trends in reproductive success of seals through annual estimates of pup production at PORE and GOGA, and 3) determine the long-term trends in sources, frequency, and level of effects of natural and anthropogenic disturbances on harbor seal haul out use and productivity.
records.title: Pinniped Monitoring Data Summaries for the San Francisco Bay Area Inventory and Monitoring Network: 1983-2026 – Data Package

records.abstract: The marine environment is increasingly polluted with a vast array of chemicals that are potential endocrine disrupters. Here, we examined the levels of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) in juvenile grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) from the Isle of May, Moray Firth (56.183293 N, -2.550398 E) and Culbin Sands (57.652778 N, -3.720833 E) between March 2016 and October 2018. Samples were collected before, during and after the first moult of their adult pelage, a period of dynamic change in fat content and fluctuating metabolic costs. Concentrations of POPs in blubber tissue are reported along with animal characteristics in the first dataset. POPs were measured at the Centre for Analytical Research and Technology at the University of Liège, Belgium and analysed after accelerated solvent extraction of the samples in hexane dichloromethane (Dionex 200 Thermo Fisher Scientific). The extracts were analysed using a gas chromatograph (Agilent 6890 GC) coupled to high resolution mass spectrometer (Autospec Ultima Mass Spectrometer Micromass). We used an ex vivo blubber explant approach to examine tissue level impacts of these intrinsic POPs in the second dataset. We measured plasma glucose and total tri-iodothyronine and thyroxine, the two major circulating thyroid hormones, with immunosorbent assays (ELISA Fortress Diagnostics Ltd) and plasma samples were sent to IDEXX laboratories for measurement of clinical chemistry and haematology parameters that are indicators of health. We exposed blubber explants overnight to either Aroclor standard mix or a high molecular weight and relatively lipophilic phthalate, benzyl butyl phthalate (BBzP), followed by a 30-minute stimulation with insulin. We used Stratagene Mx3000P qPCR System or StepOne Plus Real-Time PCR System to perform qPCR to measure gene transcript abundance of adipokines and of genes critical to the metabolism and cycling of lipids in the control and pollutant exposed explants. We measured Akt phosphorylation, a part of the insulin signalling pathway, using western blotting, using NuPAGE Bis-Tris 4-12% gradient gels (Invitrogen) followed by semi-dry transfer to a PVDF membrane and probing for total and phospho- Akt. Band density was measured using a G box imager and the Genetools software (Syngene). This work highlights the need for a better understanding and continued development of experimental methods to explore consequences of environmental chemical exposure for metabolic function in large top predators. This work was funded by Natural Environment Research Council Grants NE/M013723/1 and NE/M01357X/1 and coordinated by Dr Kimberley Bennett from Abertay University.
records.title: POP concentrations and metabolic responses to intrinsic and extrinsic polychlorinated biphenyls and benzyl butyl phthalate in grey seal juveniles from the east coast of Scotland, 2016-2018.

records.abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) present an ongoing threat to health of top predators because they are lipophilic, bioaccumulative and have endocrine disrupting properties. POPs were measured in blubber from grey seal pups (Halichoerus grypus) sampled on the Isle of May ( 56.183293, -2.550398). An ex vivo blubber explant approach was used to assess impacts of intrinsic POPs and experimental exposures to polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) on metabolic function, gene expression changes in response to key energy balance regulating hormones and insulin sensitivity of fat tissue. These datasets describe information on the grey seal pups from 3 data collection activities between October and December in 2015-2017. The blubber from these animals was used to generate tissue explants, in which we examined the effect of some typical energy balance regulating hormones (leptin, thyroid hormone, and hydrocortisone) on blubber function and gene expression (2016). Biopsies were used to create explants for overnight exposures to control media or media containing PCBs (Aroclor standard mix), with or without exposure to physiological doses of one of the three hormones (tri-iodothyronine =T3; hydrocortisone = HC; leptin = L). After explant RNA extraction, quantification (with Nanodrop 2000) and integrity checks using visual inspection after gel electrophoresis, a Stratagene Mx3000P qPCR System or StepOne Plus Real-Time PCR System was then employed for quantifying mRNA abundance of target adipose genes. Glucose, lactate and free fatty acids, were measured in media using Randox Monza colorimetric assays to assess glucose uptake, lactate production and lipolytic rate. We then examined direct effects of overnight exposure to PCB118 (a dioxin-like PCB), PCB153 (a non-dioxin like PCB) and an Aroclor mix with a POP cocktail in the presence or absence of insulin (2017), given the early results from 2016 suggesting that glucose uptake responds to dioxin-like PCBs in blubber. We measured Akt phosphorylation, a part of the insulin signalling pathway, using western blotting, using NuPAGE Bis-Tris 4-12% gradient gels (Invitrogen) followed by semi-dry transfer to a PVDF membrane and probing for total and phospho- Akt. Band density was measured using a G box imager and the Genetools software (Syngene). Intrinsic blubber POP measurement (performed at the Centre for Analytical Research and Technology at the University of Liège, Belgium) was undertaken after accelerated solvent extraction of the samples in hexane dichloromethane using a Dionex 200 column (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The extracts were analysed using a gas chromatograph (Agilent 6890 GC) coupled to a Autospec Ultima Mass Spectrometer Micromass, measuring mass transfer of pups and mothers during suckling and mass loss of the pups after weaning, thyroid hormones, and metabolite levels in the blood. Intrinsic PCBs and DDX in blubber were associated with altered metabolic function, and experimental PCB treatment altered glucose uptake in explants. The explant approach can only be used in overnight exposures, limiting the ability to infer long term consequences of altered tissue responses for whole animal energy balance. Overall, this study highlights the need to understand energy balance and its disruption by environmental chemical exposure in an increasingly polluted and exploited marine environment. This work was funded by Natural Environment Research Council Grants NE/M013723/1 and NE/M01357X/1 and coordinated by Dr Kimberley Bennett from Abertay University.
records.title: POP concentrations and metabolic responses to intrinsic and extrinsic polychlorinated biphenyls in grey seal pups from the Isle of May, Scotland, 2015-2017

records.abstract: Within the order Carnivora, the Pinnipedia sub-order is a group of marine mammals that includes sea lions, fur seals, true seals, and walruses. Pinnipeds are keystone species who serve as excellent indicators of marine ecosystem health because they respond quickly to changing oceanic conditions. Conservation concerns include effects of climate change, human disturbance, oil spills, fishing activities (operational and biological), natural and anthropogenically enhanced toxic algal blooms, preservation of haul out habitats, biomagnified contaminants, and disease. Monitoring focuses on the two numerically dominant pinniped species that breed, haul out, and molt in San Francisco Bay Area Network (SFAN) parks: the Pacific Harbor Seal (Phoca vitulina richardii) and Northern Elephant Seal (Mirounga angustirostris). This information contributes significantly to the regional and stock-wide understanding of these species required under the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972. Ancillary data on other pinniped species are collected concurrently, but are not the primary targets of this monitoring protocol. Monitoring is performed annually at two SFAN parks: Point Reyes National Seashore (PORE) and Golden Gate National Recreation Area (GOGA). Objectives are to 1) determine the long-term trends in population size and seasonal distribution of seal populations at primary sites in the SFAN parks during the breeding and molt seasons, 2) determine long-term trends in reproductive success of seals through annual estimates of pup production at PORE and GOGA, and 3) determine the long-term trends in sources, frequency, and level of effects of natural and anthropogenic disturbances on harbor seal haul out use and productivity.
records.title: Pinniped Monitoring for the NPS Inventory and Monitoring San Francisco Bay Area Network: 1983-2026 - Data Package

records.abstract: Eurasian otters are apex predators of freshwater ecosystems and a recovering species across much of their European range; investigating the dietary variation of this predator over time and space therefore provides opportunities to identify changes in freshwater trophic interactions and factors influencing the conservation of otter populations. Here we sampled faeces from 300 dead otters across England and Wales between 2007 and 2016, conducting both morphological analysis of prey remains and dietary DNA metabarcoding. Comparison of these methods showed that greater taxonomic resolution and breadth could be achieved using DNA metabarcoding but combining data from both methodologies gave the most comprehensive dietary description. All otter demographics exploited a broad range of taxa and variation likely reflected changes in prey distributions and availability across the landscape. This study provides novel insights into the trophic generalism and adaptability of otters across Britain, which is likely to have aided their recent population recovery, and may increase their resilience to future environmental changes.
records.title: Otterly delicious: Spatiotemporal variation in the diet of a recovering population of Eurasian otters (Lutra lutra) revealed through DNA metabarcoding and morphological analysis of prey remains

records.abstract: The Harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) is a highly mobile cetacean species primarily occurring in coastal and shelf waters across the Northern hemisphere. It inhabits heterogeneous seascapes broadly varying in salinity and temperature. Here, we produced 74 whole genomes at intermediate coverage to study Harbour porpoise's evolutionary history and investigate the role of local adaptation in the diversification into subspecies and populations. We identified ~6 million high quality SNPs sampled at eight localities across the North Atlantic and adjacent waters, which we used for population structure, demographic and genotype–environment association analyses. Our results suggest a genetic differentiation between three subspecies (P.p. relicta, P.p. phocoena and P.p. meridionalis), and three distinct populations within P.p. phocoena: Atlantic, Belt Sea and Proper Baltic Sea. Effective population size and Tajima's D suggest population contraction in Black Sea and Iberian porpoises, but expansion in the P.p. phocoena populations. Phylogenetic trees indicate post-glacial colonization from a southern refugium. Genotype–environment association analysis identified salinity as major driver in genomic variation and we identified candidate genes putatively underlying adaptation to different salinity. Our study highlights the value of whole genome resequencing to unravel subtle population structure in highly mobile species, shows how strong environmental gradients and local adaptation may lead to population differentiation, and how neutral and adaptive markers can give different perspectives on population subdivision. The results have great conservation implications as we found inbreeding and low genetic diversity in the endangered Black Sea subspecies and identified the critically endangered Proper Baltic Sea porpoises as a separate population.
records.title: Evolutionary history and seascape genomics of Harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) across environmental gradients in the North Atlantic and adjacent waters

records.abstract: The harbour porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) was recently classified at national level as “Critically Endangered” in Portugal, emphasising the urgent need for a dedicated conservation action plan for the population (commonly known as the Iberian porpoise population). A better understanding of the porpoise’s feeding ecology can inform appropriate conservation measures and, therefore, a combination of stomach content analysis and Stable Isotope Analysis was used to estimate the feeding ecology of harbour porpoises in Portugal over the past two decades (2003-2020). The analysis of 157 stomach contents identified Common dragonet ( Callionymus lyra ), Trisopterus spp. and Chelon spp. as the main prey species of Iberian harbour porpoise in Portuguese waters. Moreover, isotopic ratios suggested that porpoises have coastal feeding habits. Muscle isotopic ratios also suggested Trisopterus ( Trisopterus luscus were used in analysis) as the main potential prey, while hepatic stable isotopes revealed dietary variations depending on the trophic enrichment factors. Temporal and seasonal diet variations suggest that harbour porpoises may replace the predominant prey species in response to prey availability, movements within their distribution range, and/or seasonal requirements. Overall, the diet inferred from Stable Isotope Analysis was consistent with that derived from stomach content analysis, highlighting a long-term consumption of Trisopterus spp. (probably Pouting) in Portugal. In addition, this study highlights a marked overlap between fishing grounds and porpoise feeding areas, which may explain the high porpoise bycatch rates observed in northern Portugal.
records.title: Harbour porpoise feeding ecology in Portuguese waters

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how demography and natural selection interact during colonization of novel environments is a central question in evolutionary biology. The Baltic Sea region combines one of the world's strongest salinity gradients with a well‐characterized postglacial history of less than ~12,000 years. The harbour porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) is distributed across this gradient as three populations—the North Sea, Belt Sea and Proper Baltic Sea populations. Using whole genome resequencing data from 59 individuals, we reconstructed the demographic history of Baltic colonization and identified genomic signatures of local adaptation. Demographic modelling supported a sequential colonization in which the Belt Sea population diverged first from an ancestral North Sea population, followed by an independent divergence of the Proper Baltic Sea population, with two equally supported timing hypotheses placing initial colonization either during the Yoldia Sea (~11,800 years ago) or the Baltic Sea period (~8000 years ago). The Proper Baltic Sea population showed drift‐dominated divergence consistent with a founder effect, while two discrete genomic islands of differentiation with selective sweep signatures were identified between North and Belt Sea populations, pointing to recent positive selection. Both regions contain osmoregulatory candidate genes, most notably SCNN1D, encoding part of the epithelial Na + channels, a key regulator of sodium homeostasis. A non‐synonymous mutation in SCNN1D showed striking allele frequency divergence along the salinity gradient, confirmed across ~400 individuals. Together, these results reveal how genetic drift and divergent selection interact to drive rapid adaptation to a brackish environment, and identify SCNN1D as a compelling candidate for cetacean osmoregulatory adaptation.
records.title: Drift and Selection in a Recently Colonized Sea: The Genomic Basis of Adaptation to Low‐Salinity Waters in Baltic Harbour Porpoises

records.abstract: The conservation of lesser-known and data-deficient species poses significant challenges globally, particularly in developing countries such as Nepal, which harbor rich biodiversity but face resource constraints that affect scientific capacity. Furthermore, young researchers from countries such as Nepal often encounter numerous hurdles when deciding whether to pursue wildlife research or shift to other career paths. In this paper, we present a methodological approach to studying data-deficient and lesser-known species, a step-by-step roadmap that guides aspiring conservationists from step zero (the very beginning) to successfully securing sufficient funds and implementing long-lasting, impactful projects. The framework is based on a practice-oriented, experiential, and applied conservation research framework in wildlife conservation in Nepal. This framework encompasses critical steps such as species assessment, literature review, training, research planning, resource acquisition, outreach, community engagement, and conservation action planning. Case studies on the fishing cat, Eurasian otter, and owl species illustrate the practical application of these steps, highlighting successful strategies and lessons learned. The paper emphasizes the importance of collaboration, capacity building, and innovative approaches such as social media engagement and incentive-based conservation. Drawing on real-world experiences, it offers valuable insights and guidance for aspiring conservationists, providing a roadmap for navigating the complexities of wildlife conservation in resource-limited yet biodiversity-rich regions.
records.title: A practice-based approach for conservation of lesser-known species: a lesson learned from the last decade in Nepal

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Assessing foraging behavior of harbor porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) from acoustic data has become increasingly common. Yet, a wide range of analytical methods is currently used, often without formal evaluation of their comparability. This lack of cross‐method validation limits the ability to compare findings across studies and interpret differences in reported foraging activity. This study addressed this challenge by providing a systematic comparative evaluation of acoustic foraging detection methods, while introducing a novel refinement, the Search Buzz Foraging Identification (SBFI) method. We aimed to quantify the degree of similarity of the SBFI method alongside four established methods that use acoustic data and more specifically inter‐click intervals to identify foraging behavior. All methodologies were applied to the same F‐POD dataset collected at two locations for a full year. Comparability among methods was evaluated using correlation, distance, and trend analyses to assess agreement in relative patterns, absolute magnitude, and temporal dynamics. Most methods indicated strong agreement in relative foraging patterns and temporal trends; however, differences in magnitude and context‐dependent biases emerged under specific spatial or seasonal conditions, suggesting methods are not completely interchangeable. The SBFI method showed strong correlation with several existing methods while providing a comprehensive and accessible framework for identifying foraging behavior. This study gives a systemic overview of existing foraging metrics and provides a basis for improved comparability and interpretation of acoustic‐based foraging studies.
records.title: A Novel Method to Infer Harbor Porpoise Foraging Behavior From Acoustic Data: A Comparative Assessment Against Established Techniques

records.abstract: Vocal production learning is a rare skill that requires neural control over the sound production system. This control is often either laryngeal (phonatory) or supralaryngeal; in a few species, such as humans, it involves both. Recent neurobiological evidence suggests that phocine seals possess neural wiring similar to humans for laryngeal vocal learning. Within this branch, grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) can modify sounds through supralaryngeal control, but can they also control vocalizations through the larynx itself? To test this, we trained an adult male with positive reinforcement to increase the fundamental frequency (f 0) within a single vocalization, i.e. adjust its Δf 0. Using a custom-made semi-automatic setup that enabled f 0 live-tracking, we show that the seal expanded his Δf 0 from a pre-experimental median of 22.6 Hz to a median of 345 Hz in the final session, thereby demonstrating remarkable phonatory control. Our results complement behavioural evidence in other pinnipeds, showing that phocines exhibit not only respiratory and supralaryngeal control but also, as we show here, fine laryngeal control. These findings align with independent neurobiological evidence, establishing pinnipeds as a highly promising model for phonatory production learning, and introduce a new paradigm for systematically assessing respiratory, phonatory and filter control across species.
records.title: Supplementary material from "Learning without a model: extensive phonatory control in a semi-aquatic mammal"

records.abstract: This project will expand the scope of the Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission's (ANHSC) present biological sampling efforts to include subsistence hunters in communities west of Prince William Sound. The Commission is a tribal consortium concerned with self-management of the harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) as a subsistence resource. The ANHSC already conducts a biological sampling program in nine communities and participates in the harvest data assessment program with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game Subsistence Division. We plan to expand this effort to nine more communities in western Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Local technicians are selected and trained by the Commission's staff to perform basic necropsies on seals taken by subsistence hunters. Samples from these seals are sent to the University of Alaska Museum (UAM) for distribution to ongoing investigations and for archiving in the permanent collections. Tissue samples will be archived in the Alaska Frozen Tissue Collection (AFTC) which has become the primary regional archive for frozen zoological samples and a major contributor to environmental studies of the North Pacific and Arctic oceans. It is now the world's third largest frozen tissue collection for wild mammals (Hafner et al. 1997). The increasingly powerful tools of molecular biology and biochemistry and the need to monitor perturbation of the environment are accelerating both collection growth and usage. In addition to supporting expanded monitoring and sampling by the ANHSC, this project supports additional student help at UAM to process the increased number of samples. This project will increase the scope of sampling from a protected and potentially threatened high-trophic-level subsistence resource, and increase the scope of Native involvement in the study and management of marine resources. This project also includes; Gordon Jarrell, University of Alaska Fairbanks, P.O. Box 757220, Fairbanks, Alaska 99775-7220, fnghj@uaf.edu Monica Riedel, Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission, P.O. records.abstract: Protected areas are expected to provide suitable habitats for wildlife even within human-altered landscapes, but environmental cues can be misleading. We evaluated whether a strictly protected, rehabilitated marshland (Kis-Balaton, KB) acts as an ecological trap for the Eurasian otter ( Lutra lutra ), a sentinel apex predator. Using non-invasive genetic sampling within the marshland (90 individuals) and nationwide post-mortem monitoring (462 individuals), we found a spatially heterogeneous population, with a genetically insulated peripheral group. Kinship and group sex ratios indicated kin-structured residents, among which frequent attack-related injuries were consistent with strong territorial behaviour. Net gene flow was directed towards the marshland's core area, mainly via the Zala River. However, immigrants were mainly detected in peripheral areas near settlements and roads, where recovered carcasses showed a higher prevalence of attack-related injuries (KB: 35.7%, other regions: 13.1%), and body condition was poorer in injured than in uninjured otters. These patterns indicate that immigrants rarely integrate into the resident population. The core population remains demographically viable, so the marshland is not a classical ecological trap but a dead-end for dispersers rather than a true refuge. Failure of immigrants to establish, despite apparent habitat connectivity, suggests intrinsic constraints that may be set by the area's ecological carrying capacity. We recommend restoring habitat connectivity, improving legal protection and suitability of small watercourses, and implementing road mitigation and free-ranging dog control to reduce mortality risks. These actions are crucial for gene flow and long-term otter population viability in wetland ecosystems.
records.title: All that glitters is not gold: genetic and post-mortem monitoring indicate dispersal risks for a semi-aquatic apex predator in a protected marshland

records.abstract: During the late summer of 1997, for the first time ever recorded, most of the continental shelf of the eastern Bering Sea was covered by aquamarine waters (Figure 1) which resulted from a massive bloom of coccolithophores (Figure 2). Reflectance of light off the calcium carbonate plates of the flagellated coccolithophores gave the water its anomalous color, which was first observed in July. The bloom was also clearly visible from space, as shown by some of the first images from the multispectral SeaWiFS scanner in September. Light penetration into the water column, essential for primary production by diatoms and other Phytoplankton, was markedly reduced. This shift in the dominant primary producers potentially altered the trophic dynamics throughout the food web of one of world's most productive ecosystems. Prior to and during the bloom, anomalous atmospheric and oceanic conditions were evident. In July, large whales were relatively abundant in the region of the middle shelf where the bloom occurred. Concomitant with the bloom of coccolithophores were die offs of seabirds and a decrease in the number of salmon returning to Bristol Bay. Reports of die-offs of seabirds began in early August. Field operations conducted as part of the National Science Foundation's Inner Front project and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Coastal Ocean Program and Fisheries Oceanography Coordinated Investigations provide a wealth of data to explore this year's anomalous conditions. The eastern Bering Sea shelf (Figure 3) consists of domains characterized by water properties, water column structure and plankton dynamics. Coastal water (depth less than 50 m) is typically mixed by a combination of tidal and wind stirring. Water over the middle shelf (depth 50-100 m) usually has two well mixed layers: the upper a result of the annual melt of sea ice and/or solar heating while the lower remains cold and rich in nutrients essential for Phytoplankton growth. Separating the domains is a structure or inner front which extends for over 1000 km around the shelf. The dynamics of the inner front likely provide nitrogenous nutrients for the prolonged primary and secondary production which typically occurs there. Typical springtime Phytoplankton blooms in the Bering Sea are comprised of diatoms and are associated with increased water column stratification as a result of sea-ice meltback or solar radiation. Summertime Phytoplankton blooms of the magnitude observed this year are rare, in part because the nutrients for plant growth are generally thought to be limiting. Zooplankton biomass may be enhanced two different ways: increased secondary production via increased food availability for herbivorous grazers, and physical concentration of grazers due to convergence of water at the front. As a result of the favorable conditions generated by this increase in prey biomass, massive flocks of seabirds return each year to feed at the front and breed in Alaskan waters. A sequence of unusual phenomena occurred in the coupled atmosphere-ice-ocean system this year which may have favored rapid growth of the coccolithophores. Winter sea ice conditions exhibited average areal and latitudinal extent but melt back appeared to be unusually rapid. In spring and summer, there were reduced numbers of energetic storms and anomalously cloud free conditions. One consequence was that greater stratification than usual occurred over the shelf. Sea surface temperatures were up to 3￸ C above normal in June. The decrease in storms and clouds resulted from atmospheric connections to the current El Nino occurring in the equatorial Pacific. The warm waters were not due to a direct oceanic connection to the ongoing El Nino. Aquamarine waters were first observed in early July. By this time, the normal summer Phytoplankton community had probably been replaced by coccolithophores. Characteristic of these blooms is surface waters that have high reflectance, low chlorophyll and particulate organic carbon concentrations. Light penetration and visibility in the aquamarine waters were markedly reduced, with Secchi depths of one-third normal being observed (2 meters in bloom areas versus about 6 meters in non-bloom areas). Light extinction coefficients at Nunivak Island, as determined by the PAR sensor on the CTD (conductivity, temperature, depth measurements), doubled from June to August (0.07/meter in June and 0.14/meter in August). By September, the areal extent of the bloom was 700x300 kilometers. The vertical extent of the bloom, based on underwater video observations made in September, varied from a thin layer to a layer up to 50 meters deep. In some areas near shore the layer extended to the sea floor. At that time the bloom had been evident for two months which is longer than most recorded blooms. The conditions near the inner front off Cape Newenham provide an example of the abnormal conditions. In June, nitrogenous nutrients were depleted from the bottom layer of the middle shelf and the inner front was not well developed. Short-tailed shearwaters (Puffinus tenuirostris), however, were eating their normal diet of adult euphausiids and had normal body weights. In mid-July, densities of seabirds were lower in the eastern edge of the aquamarine waters of outer Bristol Bay. In general, however, the condition and behavior of pelagic seabirds was normal during July. Large feeding flocks of short-tailed shearwaters were observed on the middle shelf. By the first week of August, coastal die-offs of birds were reported. During the late summer and early fall, a major die-off occurred with thousands of dead birds washing ashore. In the fall, observations near the Pribilof Islands and off Nunivak Island substantiated the reports. Corpses of birds were conspicuous in areas affected by the bloom. Both dead and living shearwaters had significantly reduced body mass compared to birds collected in June, indicating starvation. In addition to the typical diet for shearwaters in Bristol Bay of euphausiids, fish and squid were also being ingested. Those birds ingesting euphausiids were preying upon the smaller juvenile stages. Additionally, foraging shearwaters appeared to avoid areas with aquamarine water (both around the inner fronts and at the Pribilof Islands), where they may have had difficulty in detecting and capturing prey under the existing low underwater light conditions. Given the observations to date, we believe starvation was the prime cause of the shearwater die-off. Other changes were evident in the ecosystem. The Bristol Bay salmon run was at least 15 million fish below predictions. Evidence from a test fishery at Port Moller suggests that the fish were dying on their way to Bristol Bay. Salmon were found to be more common in the diets of the northern fur seal than in previous years. Redistributions of some species of whales in the southeast Bering Sea may have occurred, but there are few large-scale synoptic surveys of cetaceans available for comparison during the past 20 years. During July, five species of large whales (humpback whales - Megaptera novaeangliae, fin whale - Balaenoptera physalus, sei whale - Balaenoptera borealis, minke whale - Balaenoptera acutorostrata, and right whale - Eubalaena glacialis) and harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) were observed either in or near the coccolithophore bloom on the middle shelf. This suggests that the bloom and adjacent waters provided productive foraging for cetaceans and their prey. Comparison of this year with more normal years in the future will be needed to confirm the changes in feeding behavior. records.abstract: This project will expand the scope of the Alaska Native Harbor Seal Commission's (ANHSC) present biological sampling efforts to include subsistence hunters in communities west of Prince William Sound. The Commission is a tribal consortium concerned with self-management of the harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) as a subsistence resource. The ANHSC already conducts a biological sampling program in nine communities and participates in the harvest data assessment program with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game Subsistence Division. We plan to expand this effort to nine more communities in western Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Local technicians are selected and trained by the Commission's staff to perform basic necropsies on seals taken by subsistence hunters. Samples from these seals are sent to the University of Alaska Museum (UAM) for distribution to ongoing investigations and for archiving in the permanent collections. Tissue samples will be archived in the Alaska Frozen Tissue Collection (AFTC) which has become the primary regional archive for frozen zoological samples and a major contributor to environmental studies of the North Pacific and Arctic oceans. It is now the world's third largest frozen tissue collection for wild mammals (Hafner et al. 1997). The increasingly powerful tools of molecular biology and biochemistry and the need to monitor perturbation of the environment are accelerating both collection growth and usage. In addition to supporting expanded monitoring and sampling by the ANHSC, this project supports additional student help at UAM to process the increased number of samples. This project will increase the scope of sampling from a protected and potentially threatened high-trophic-level subsistence resource, and increase the scope of Native involvement in the study and management of marine resources. This poses a risk to long-term sustainability.Fishery closures have been established that are a step toward protecting the ecoregion’s diverse benthic habitats and vulnerable marine ecosystems (VME) from disturbance by bottom-contacting fishing gear.To a lesser extent, wastewater and shipping pose a risk to all ecosystem components by releasing marine litter, namely microplastics and other contaminants.The risks posed by wastewater are aggravated by limited wastewater treatment infrastructures. Pressures associated with shipping are anticipated to increase in the ecoregion.State of the ecosystemPrimary production is high in Icelandic waters, and phytoplankton biomass is increasing on the south Iceland shelf.Stocks of northern shrimp (Pandalus borealis), Norway lobster (Nephrops norvegicus), Atlantic halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus), and beaked redfish (Sebastes mentella) remain below historical biomass levels, while the biomasses of mackerel (Scomber scombrus) and Norwegian spring spawning herring (Clupea harengus) are below target.Populations of fulmars (Fulmarus glacialis) and kittiwakes (Rissa tridactyla) continue to decline in the ecoregion.The status of harbour seal (Phoca vitulina) remains a conservation concern in the ecoregion.Recent changes in capelin (Mallotus villosus) abundance and distribution are expected to have important consequences on Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), seabirds, and whales in the ecoregion.Climate changeSurface and bottom waters of the Iceland shelf have warmed by > 1.1°C since 1975, primarily due to increased northward transport of Atlantic Water into the ecoregion.Warming is most pronounced in surface waters in the north, where a shift in zooplankton community composition from Arctic to boreal large copepod taxa is evident.Rising temperatures have contributed to the decline of northern shrimp and Iceland scallop (Chlamys islandica) populations, to the shifting capelin distribution beyond the Iceland shelf, and to groundfish species moving northward or to deeper waters.Surface water pH is declining on the shelf. Acidification effects on marine biota and habitats are largely unknown and are a key concern in the ecoregion.Warming is projected to continue and result in the spatial redistribution of commercially harvested species on the Iceland shelf.Environmental and socio-economic contextFisheries significantly contribute to national revenues and employment and have high cultural importance in the ecoregion.Balancing economic and social benefits from fisheries with ecosystem conservation objectives is a key trade-off in the ecoregion.The rapid growth of tourism, shipping, and finfish aquaculture is raising additional societal concerns and trade-offs among marine sectors and associated pressures.

records.abstract: Incidental bycatch of harbour porpoise ( Phocoena phocoena ) in set-net fisheries poses a threat to their populations. Pingers, acoustic devices designed to deter cetaceans, are currently the primary tool used to reduce porpoise bycatch without impeding fishing effort. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of different pinger spacing configurations at reducing porpoise bycatch in the Danish North Sea turbot ( Scophthalmus maximus ) fishery. Three trials were conducted in 2021, 2023, and 2025, testing standard Banana pingers with varying spacings of 200 m and 500 m (B-200 and B-500, respectively), and a third alternative using a louder Banana pinger version (LB-500) with a 500 m spacing. Another, even louder, pinger type (DDDs) was tested only in 2025 with a spacing of 1,800 m. Results from the combined trials indicated that B-200 reduced bycatch per unit effort (BPUE) by 66%, B-500 reduced BPUE by 30% and STM-1800 reduced BPUE by 52%. Across years, pingers showed inconsistent results. B-200 reduced porpoise bycatch by 56% in 2023 and by 73% in 2025, while B-500 reduced bycatch by 55% only in 2025. LB-500 reduced bycatch by 74% in 2025, and STM-1800 reduced bycatch by 64% in 2025. These results show that, while increasing pinger spacing reduces pinger implementation costs, effectiveness declines significantly unless the pinger's source level is increased. This research underscores the need for precise pinger spacing regulations to effectively reduce harbour porpoise bycatch.
records.title: MIND THE GAP: Pingers, spacing, and sound levels influence bycatch rates of harbour porpoises

records.abstract: Introduction: Toxoplasma gondii oocysts shed in the feces of cats and other felids (definitive hosts) are resistant in the environment, particularly in seawater. They can remain infectious for several months and serve as a source of contamination for marine mammals. The objective of our study is to assess the prevalence of T. gondii in marine mammals stranded between 2010 and 2023 on the French metropolitan coasts, and to characterize the genetic diversity of the infecting strains.Materials/Methods: A total of 60 muscle samples were collected, including 43 common dolphins (Delphinus delphis), 6 bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus), 5 harbor porpoises (Phocoena phocoena), 3 striped dolphins (Stenella coeruleoalba), 1 long-finned pilot whale (Globicephala melas), 1 gray seal (Halichoerus grypus), and 1 Cuvier’s beaked whale (Ziphius cavirostris). A modified agglutination test (MAT) on meat juice and a direct qPCR (529 RE and B1) on DNA extracted from the sampled tissues, were performed, followed by a microsatellite genotyping when possible.Results: The overall seroprevalence was of 56.7% (34/60) with a specific seroprevalence for common dolphins of 69.8% (30/43) while two harbor porpoises and two bottlenose dolphins were seropositive. Quantitative PCR confirmed the presence of T. gondii in 8 of the 30 seropositive common dolphins. Three isolates were genotyped, revealing type II genotypes. By comparing these genotypes with published data and the French National Reference Centre forToxoplasmosis database, the strains were found to be closely related to type II strains isolated from a French and a Turkish patients and a French pig, differing by only 1–3 markers.Conclusions: The high seroprevalence of T. gondii in marine mammals, particularly in common dolphins, suggests significant contamination of the sea by oocysts. The identification of three genotypes belonging to the type II lineage predominant in Europe provides evidence of circulation between terrestrial and marine environment, particularly through the leaching of soil contaminated by feces from infected cats. The results concerning certain species should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of samples, hence the need for a larger study to better understand the risk factors and ecological implications.
records.title: Prevalence and genotypes of Toxoplasma gondii in marine mammals of France

records.abstract: Harbor Porpoises occur regularly in the north Pacific Ocean and the Bering Sea and occasionally in the Chukchi Sea during the ice-free months. Point Barrow, Alaska is considered to be near the northern limit of distribution for this species. We have obtained nine records from the vicinity of Point Barrow between 1985 and 1991. Harbor Porpoises were found entangled in subsistence fishing nets, seen live or found dead on the beach. These records indicate a regular use of the northeastern Chukchi Sea and extreme western Beaufort Sea. The reasons for their occurrence near Point Barrow are unknown but the relative abundance of fish in coastal arctic lagoons may attract Harbor Porpoises northward. records.abstract: ABSTRACT The Eurasian otter ( Lutra lutra ) is a semiaquatic, freshwater top predator of conservation concern due to its significant global population decline in the last century. Following its recovery and recolonization in parts of Europe, the population faces ongoing threats, including habitat loss and fragmentation due to human activities, climate change, prey depletion, and exposure to emerging contaminants. Accurately identifying its diet is crucial for understanding ecological interactions and proposing effective management strategies. DNA metabarcoding based on high‐throughput sequencing is a reliable diet analysis tool with better resolution than traditional methods. This study, for the first time, applied two 16S rRNA primers targeting different prey classes on the dietary spectrum of two Eurasian otters populations returning to Northern Germany (Schleswig‐Holstein and Lower Saxony). DNA fragments of prey items from the gut contents of 156 otters collected between 2005 and 2022 were sequenced. Fifty‐five operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were identified in the dietary remains, including freshwater and marine fish, anurans, caudates, and water birds. Otters in the study area are opportunistic predators with wide dietary plasticity, feeding on the most abundant species. Nine‐spined sticklebacks, common roach, and common frogs were important prey items, and marine fish species were detected in the diet of some of the investigated otters. The otters' diet differed between Lower Saxony and Schleswig‐Holstein, between sexes, and a slight difference was observed between adults and subadults. This study provides new insights into the diet composition of otters and their ability to exploit a variety of resources in their habitat. This information is vital for understanding their chances of survival in an environment that is continuously changing due to human impacts and for developing effective management tools.
records.title: Guts and Glory: Unraveling the Diet of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra lutra ) Populations Using DNA Metabarcoding of Gut Contents

records.abstract: ABSTRACT Kashmir Valley is a unique landscape nestled in the northwest Himalaya. It is a flat‐bottomed valley flanked on all sides by mountains. The valley is drained by the River Jhelum, which is fed by an extensive network of tributaries. The valley was once an uncontested abode of Eurasian otters. However, for the past many decades, no sighting of the animal was reported until recently. Hunting, habitat destruction, and pollution were the main reasons for pushing the population into decline. This paper collates the recent reports of Eurasian Otter sightings from the valley after decades, establishing the re‐emergence of the otters in the valley. This brings a propitious moment for ecological health and resilience. It further outlines the possible threats that have emerged recently and will impact the otter population's re‐emergence severely. The study also highlights the need for conservation to firmly re‐establish otters as top predators of Kashmir's freshwater ecosystems and the means of achieving the otter conservation goals.
records.title: Re‐Emergence of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra Lutra ) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge

records.abstract: Ecological and environmental drivers shape evolution, yet little is known about the molecular underpinnings of adaptation. Omics tools (e.g. genomics and transcriptomics) can help us understand the mechanisms of long-term trait evolution, such as lactation strategies, and shorter-term population dynamics. Pinnipeds (seals, sea lions, fur seals, and walruses), a closely related monophyletic group, represent some of the most extreme and diverse lactation strategies known. This trait diversity stems from their worldwide distribution across a wide range of habitats and latitudes, and their obligate spatiotemporal separation of land and sea for breeding and foraging. In this thesis, we uncover signals of molecular evolution of key lactation traits in pinnipeds using comparative functional genomics and comparative transcriptomics. We identify candidate changes in pathways linked to mammary involution and lipid metabolism, and reveal coordinated expression of genes involved in lipid mobilisation, energy balance, high fat milk, and mother-to-pup energy transfer. Novel grey seal transcriptomes for milk fat, blubber, and pup blubber were generated from collections made in early (day 5) and late (day 15) lactation on the Isle of May 2023. Along with uncovering the protein properties of key milk fat globule membrane genes, we obtained the first physical properties of milk fat globules in grey seals – allowing us to investigate mechanisms of milk emulsion stability in high fat milk. Our findings show that seal milk contains exceptionally small globules with weakened net surface charge, offering a potential mechanism for stabilising high-fat milk. Finally, we reconstructed the demographic history and genetic health of Caspian seals, showing that changes in effective population size track major paleoenvironmental shifts while recent inbreeding remains low, providing direction for future conservation strategies. Overall, the findings presented in this thesis represent an important foundation for future omics studies targeting marine mammal biology, and offer a lens into understanding eco-evolutionary trajectories of populations and extreme phenotypes.

records.abstract: Between October 8 and October 15, 2026, an operational field vehicle operated by MobiCom Corporation—a consolidated Mongolian telecommunications subsidiary of Japan's KDDI Corporation—ignited dry steppe vegetation during fiber-optic border station maintenance in eastern Mongolia's Dornod Province. The resulting wildfire burned approximately 530,000 ha (~5,300 sq km, or 2.4x the area of Metropolitan Tokyo), consuming 79.8% of the Numrug Strictly Protected Area (a critical refuge for Ussuri moose, Eurasian otter, and 263 avian species) and advancing to the Inner Mongolia border of the People's Republic of China, where 606 Mongolian and 3,400 Chinese personnel were mobilized. Treating this ecological catastrophe merely as an unverified Profit-and-Loss (P&L) extraordinary indemnity expense (L_P&L) exposes the parent corporation and Japanese sovereign diplomacy to compounding cross-border geopolitical friction, Mongolian public backlash, and severe Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) penalties under Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) LEAP and Sustainability Standards Board of Japan (SSBJ) statutory filings. Building directly upon the sovereign agro-ecological architecture established in Zenodo Monograph 10.5281/zenodo.23654305, this monograph formulates a deterministic four-pillar Sovereign Nature-Positive Restoration Protocol tailored to the Mongolian steppe ecosystem. First, we prove Theorem 2.1 (Steppe Balance-Sheet Environmental Assetization), converting deadweight P&L indemnity losses into capitalized Balance-Sheet (B/S) ecological restoration infrastructure assets (Delta A_env) coupled with Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) Methodology JP-MN-STEPPE-01 for rotational grazing and Soil Organic Carbon (Delta C_SOC) sequestration bundled with nomadic "Five Snouts" (Tavan Khoshuu Mal, H_k) polygon traceability (P_k). Second, we formalize a Sovereign Digital Public Goods Barter deploying Japan's JAXA ALOS-4 (DAICHI-4) PALSAR-3 L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (200 km swath, 3 m resolution) to penetrate smoke and cloud cover, providing the Mongolian Ministry of Environment and Climate Change with cryptographic burn-severity mapping and neutralizing cross-border disinformation while executing Paris Agreement Article 6.2 Corresponding Adjustments (alpha_ITMO). Third, we embed deterministic hardware interlocks (PHOENIX_BRIDGE x QFS-zkVM over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field F_p, p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1) into maintenance vehicles and telecom base stations, enforcing sub-0.5 ms RTO P2.0 thermal/geofence ignition cutoffs and 2/3 Human-in-Command (HIC) threshold authorization. Fourth, we establish Proposition 5.1 and Theorem 5.1, proving how zero-knowledge spatial verification (rho_verified -> 1) eliminates the SSBJ/TNFD unverified risk multiplier (kappa_penalty >= 4.0) and satisfies board fiduciary oversight mandates under Delaware Caremark and Japan's Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA). records.abstract: The Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra), a semi-aquatic carnivore listed as “Near Threatened” by the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), is widespread across Eurasia but remains poorly studied genetically in various regions. We analyzed the Central Anatolian population along the Kızılırmak River using mitochondrial (mt) DNA from non-invasively collected samples to examine whether Anatolian otters connect phylogenetically typical European and Caucasian lineages and whether Anatolia could have harbored a late-glacial source population for otter migration to Europe via western (Balkan) and/or eastern (east of the Black Sea) routes. Thirty spraints were collected from five localities, including four previously known sites and one newly identified in the Sulakyurt district, northeast of Kırıkkale province. We amplified a short (256 bp) mtD-loop fragment and a longer (820 bp) fragment spanning the Cytb, tRNA-Thr, tRNA-Pro, and D-loop from 14 samples and included all corresponding Lutra lutra mtDNA sequences available in GenBank in our analyses. Six short-fragment samples from Kapulukaya, Kesikköprü, and Kalecik carried the widespread northern Eurasian haplotype Lut1, while eight samples from Kalecik, Kesikköprü, Hirfanlı, and Hamzalı revealed a novel haplotype (H256-TR). The long fragments represented two additional haplotypes (H820-37, H820-38), distributed across the same localities. Median-joining network analysis of the short fragment produced a star-like topology with no clear phylogeographic structuring, whereas the longer fragment resolved two weakly separated phylogenetic groups. Central Anatolian haplotypes were positioned between Far Eastern and northern Eurasian lineages, with H820-38 phylogenetically connecting Caucasian and European haplotypes. This finding is consistent with the hypothesis of possible western and eastern postglacial migration routes from Anatolia to Europe, although broader spatial sampling is needed for confirmation.
records.title: Mitochondrial DNA Lineages of Eurasian Otters (Lutra lutra) in Central Anatolia: A Phylogenetic Bridge Between Asia and Europe?

records.abstract: The harbor seal ( Phoca vitulina ) is a sentinel top predator in the North Sea, inhabiting regions with high shipping activity. The rapid expansion of offshore wind farms (OWFs) is expected to further increase vessel traffic and underwater noise levels. The population-relevant behavioral consequences for harbor seals remain difficult to infer from tagging or visual surveys alone due to limited sample sizes, uneven coverage, and strong interindividual variability. This chapter presents a methodological framework that couples a large-scale, time-varying vessel noise soundscape with a telemetry-informed agent-based model (ABM) to explore potential future scenarios and mitigation efforts. Behavioral parameters were derived from 13 seals equipped with sound and movement sensing biologgers (DTAGs). Simulated animals were programmed with empirically derived parameters within four defined behavioral states, while the behavioral response functions are integrated as state-probability modifiers. Four scenarios are defined: a 2018 baseline, OWF-2030 and OWF-2050 traffic projections, and a speed-reduction policy within marine protected areas. The chapter provides a reproducible blueprint for constructing, parameterizing, and coupling soundscape and ABM components, enabling transparent what-if analyses beyond the reach of observational studies.
records.title: Harbor Seal Behavior Under Shipping Noise: A Coupled Soundscape and Agent-Based Modeling Approach

records.abstract: The effect of a pinger designed to reduce cetacean bycatch in fisheries on the behavior of a harbor porpoise was quantified through exposure experiments in a pool. The “banana pinger” (Fishtek Marine Ltd.) sounds were comprised of signal blocks (duration ~0.5 s), each containing four frequency components (8–125 kHz; peak 70 kHz). Sounds were played back at mean received levels of 83, 89, 95, 101, and 107 dB re 1 μPa. Behavioral responses, including increased respiration rate, jumping, and swimming faster and farther away from the source, occurred from 95 dB re 1 μPa. At sea, distances at which harbor porpoises are deterred by pingers will depend on environmental parameters influencing sound propagation. Based on this study with a captive individual, wild porpoises should hear the “banana pinger” sounds at a greater distance than the deterring distance, so sounds may alert them and reduce their likelihood of entanglement. Pingers should be easy to use, reliable, and durable. Cost, sound pollution, directionality, habituation, and audibility to seals and fish should be minimized; range and deterring effect should be optimized. Due to its behavioral effect on harbor porpoises, the “banana pinger” appears to be effective.
records.title: Reducing Fisheries Bycatch: Behavioral Responses of a Harbor Porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) in a Pool to the Sounds of a “Banana Pinger”

records.abstract: The first large scale decommissioning projects of offshore wind farms are planned in Europe in the coming 5 years. The underwater sound generated during the decommissioning phase of offshore wind farms remains poorly understood due to the limited number of such projects conducted to date. Nevertheless, activities associated with decommissioning have the potential to impact marine life. This study is the first to present acoustic effect ranges from decommissioning activities associated with the removal of a 1.8 m diameter monopile by abrasive cutting and assessing their potential impact on the harbour porpoise. Two JASCO Multi-Channel Acoustic Recorders, equipped with two hydrophones, were deployed for ~10 days in November 2024. The potential impact ranges on relevant marine fauna calculated for three key operations were studied: jacking-up of the vessel, dredging down-the-hole and cutting. The permanent threshold shift onset threshold was never exceeded by any of the operations. Both dredging and cutting exceeded the VHF weighted temporary threshold shift (TTS, L E = 153 dB re 1 μPa 2 s according to Southall et al. (2019) and 161 dB re 1 μPa 2 s according to the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).
records.title: Store Middelgrund Monopile Removal: How Far Can Sound Emissions from Decommissioning Impact on the Harbour Porpoise?
